items: Fan-out: one input channel, N goroutines receiving
The runtime load-balances; a free worker takes next
Fast workers naturally take more, with no extra code

lines: close(jobs) // all N range loops exit

items: One `close(jobs)` terminates all N workers
A close broadcasts to every blocked receiver at once
`errgroup.Group` with `g.SetLimit(n)` is the modern shape
It bounds the fan-out and propagates the first error
Alternative: one goroutine per job gated by a size-N semaphore
Results arrive in completion order, not submission order
Need order? Attach the input index to each result
Sort by that index at the consumer, never in a worker
The results reader must keep up with the workers
A stalled reader blocks their sends and stalls the fan-out
Buffer `jobs` at N so the dispatcher stays a round ahead

lines: err error // one chan, sane ordering

blocks.title: Anti-Pattern
blocks.text: An unbounded `go` per item over a large input: thousands of goroutines all hitting one database is a self-inflicted outage.

items: Fan-in: N input channels merged into one output
A single consumer reads the merged stream
A naive select handles a fixed two or three inputs
It does not generalise to a slice of channels

lines: out := make(chan T, len(cs)) // one slot each

items: The `wg.Wait()` closer goroutine is mandatory
Capture the loop variable or all goroutines share one
Output order is nondeterministic and interleaved
Fan-in gives you completion order, nothing more
Merging is a select over a changing set of channels
`reflect.Select` does that selection at runtime
It is slow and reflective, so rarely worth it
Each stage closes its own output channel
Each stage stops sending when `done` or `ctx` closes
Stages chain by channels alone, nothing shared
The consumer returns early and stops reading `out`
Every merge goroutine blocks forever on `out <- v`
One leaked goroutine per input channel, until exit

lines: case out <- v: // consumer still reading
go func(c <-chan T) { // pass it in
for v := range c { out <- v }

items: Pre-Go 1.22 the goroutines all shared one `c`
Every merge goroutine then drained the same input
Passing the channel as a parameter fixes it

blocks.title: Size And Rate
blocks.text: Buffer `out` at `len(cs)` so each producer can place one item without waiting. Rate-limit at the fan-in point with one ticker, not N throttled producers.

items: Leak 1: a sender blocked forever, receiver returned early
Always pair a send with a `ctx.Done()` case
Leak 2: `for range ch` on a channel nobody closes
That goroutine parks until the process exits
`go.uber.org/goleak` in tests catches strays
Or assert `runtime.NumGoroutine()` before and after
Run with `-race`: it catches misuse of sent pointers
It does not check the channel operations themselves

blocks.title: Silent Deadlock
blocks.text: `fatal error: all goroutines are asleep - deadlock!` fires only when every goroutine is blocked. A partial deadlock is completely silent.

items: `v, ok := <-ch` and `for range ch` observe a close
They are the only two correct ways from the receive side
A bare receive cannot tell zero value from closed
THE RULE: only a sender closes, and only if it is solo
Never let a receiver close a channel it reads
Many senders? Never close from inside one of them
Use a `done` channel, `sync.Once`, or a closer goroutine
Buffered values survive a close; receivers drain first
Closing wakes every goroutine blocked on receive
That broadcast is how one `done` cancels N workers

blocks.title: Worked Example
blocks.text: Call `close(results)` before the workers finish and the next `results <- r` gives `panic: send on closed channel`, taking the whole process down.

items: Channels are not always the answer
A counter wants `sync/atomic`; state wants `sync.Mutex`
Signal-only channels should be `chan struct{}`
Zero allocation and the intent is unmistakable
select waits on many channel operations at once
Several ready? It picks one uniformly at random
`default:` makes the whole select non-blocking

blocks.title: Timer Leak
blocks.text: `case <-time.After(2*time.Second)` leaks its timer until it fires. In a hot loop use `time.NewTimer` with `defer t.Stop()` instead.

items: A closed input stays ready and busy-spins the loop
Nil the variable and select drops that case for good

lines: // loop while a != nil || b != nil

items: Do not park a channel in a struct field casually
Only when that struct owns its whole lifecycle
Ambiguous ownership is what causes double closes

blocks.title: The Whole Handbook
blocks.text: Unbuffered is synchronization, buffered is queueing with a ceiling, close is a broadcast, nil is an off switch, and select composes them all.

caption.text: Part 2 of GO CHANNELS: FIELD NOTES. Most Go concurrency bugs are not race conditions — they are one goroutine parked forever on a send nobody will ever receive. These ten pages are the whole channel model: unbuffered rendezvous, buffer sizing that is a memory ceiling rather than a perf knob, the hchan fast path, the three ways close panics, and the nil-channel trick that turns select into a switchboard. Save it for the next time a worker pool quietly stops.
